rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

examples: This non-opening story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit.
This story card has three sentences: the opening question, the drawer joke and the statement about the people crying out. Non-opening story cards are limited to two.
This story card has three sentences, exceeding the two-sentence limit for a non-opening story card.

rule.text: The rule against guessing the next words of a line (see below) applies to every passage, and to fill in the blank too. The blank tests meaning the baker can reason out, not wording they haven't seen.

examples: The setup only gives the challenge "Who then is like Me?" It does not establish that the proof concerns declaring the future, so the baker cannot reason out "foretell" rather than "control" or "prevent." The blank tests wording that has not yet been shown.
The preceding story card says only that the man burns "some" of the wood. That gives no basis for reasoning out the exact proportion "half" in the first blank, so that blank tests unseen wording.

The blank asks for the exact unseen wording of Isaiah 54:6. The preceding cards stop at Isaiah 54:5 and provide no storyteller setup about the deserted wife, so this is a next-word fill-in rather than a question about the passage's movement or meaning.

Both blanks ask the baker to supply the exact wording of an unseen line from Isaiah 54:7. There is no preceding story card establishing this moment, so the baker is filling in the prophet's words rather than reasoning through a setup.

The blank asks for the exact next word in Isaiah 54:15's statement that the attacker will fall before the city. The preceding story card says only that an attack would not be from the LORD; it does not establish the attacker's outcome, leaving the baker to guess the line's wording.
Card 6 says only that He has trodden the winepress; it gives no context from which to infer "alone." The blank therefore asks the baker to guess the next unheard word of the line.

The earlier cards establish that no one helped, but they do not introduce the arm picture or give a sufficient basis for choosing "arm" over "voice" or "name." The blank asks for unseen wording rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.
The earlier cards give no basis for choosing pigs over lambs or goats. The blank asks for an unseen detail rather than meaning the baker can reason out.
Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker reason that the second group is their fathers. This is a guess at wording the baker has not seen.
The preceding card only describes the servants' joy and the others' wailing. It gives no basis for choosing name over land or silver, so the blank tests unseen wording.

The earlier cards only say that the brothers are brought from the nations, list their transportation and identify Jerusalem. They give no basis for reasoning that the brothers are brought as a gift, so this blank asks for wording from verse 20 that the baker has not seen rather than a meaning supported by the setup.
Nothing before this card indicates the pot's direction, so north is an unseen word chosen by luck from three directions rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

The earlier cards name the star Wormwood and tell where it falls, but they do not establish what wormwood is like or what happens to the waters. The baker cannot reason out that the missing word is bitter.
The blanks ask for seven heads and ten horns before either number has been disclosed or made inferable. The baker can only guess these unseen details, especially the ten horns.
Nothing in the earlier cards lets the baker infer "marvel" rather than "mourn" or "flee." The blank asks for an unseen verb rather than a meaning the baker can reason out.

The blank asks for an unrevealed word from the verse. Nothing in the preceding cards about God's dwelling with His people lets the baker reason out that the word is tear rather than merely guess the wording.

The baker has not been given enough context to reason out which group belongs in the blank. The preceding card supplies the twelve gates, their angels, and later the tribes' names, but nothing that makes apostles of the Lamb inferable for the foundations; this tests unrevealed wording.

Card 6 says only that Jesus identifies the testimony's recipients. Nothing in the earlier cards gives the baker a basis for choosing "churches" over "kings" or "nations," so this blank asks for wording the baker has not seen rather than a meaning they can reason out.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

examples: The question begins "He burns" without identifying the woodworker. Once the preceding story card is off screen, the pronoun has no self-contained context.
The question relies on "He" and "that wood" instead of identifying the woodworker and the wood he used. It depends on earlier cards that are no longer visible rather than supplying its own context.
The question depends on "that wild donkey" in the preceding story card and does not identify the donkey as a picture of Israel. It does not supply enough context on its own.

places.problem: The question begins "He burns" without identifying the woodworker. Once the preceding story card is off screen, the pronoun has no self-contained context.
The question relies on "He" and "that wood" instead of identifying the woodworker and the wood he used. It depends on earlier cards that are no longer visible rather than supplying its own context.
The question depends on "that wild donkey" in the preceding story card and does not identify the donkey as a picture of Israel. It does not supply enough context on its own.
The question never identifies who "them" and "they" refer to. Without the preceding story card, it does not make clear that the LORD is judging Israel.
The question begins "That silver and gold," using "that" to point back to the previous story card instead of restating the context, such as the silver from Tarshish and gold from Uphaz.
The question uses "that wound" and "it" to point back to the preceding story card instead of supplying the wound's context within the question itself.

Cards 4, 10 and 11 use "their" or "them" without identifying the people, and card 6 begins with "that oath" even though its antecedent was on the preceding story card. These questions rely on cards that are no longer visible instead of supplying their own context.

Card 8 does not identify who "these people" are, card 12 refers back to "that beautiful olive tree" without establishing the picture in the question, and card 13 does not identify who "the people" are. These questions are not self-contained once the preceding story cards disappear.
"That nation" points back to the preceding story card. Without that card, the question does not retell the setup that the LORD had announced He would build up and establish the nation.

The question asks why the LORD says "this" without restating the wormwood and poisoned-water judgment. It relies on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible, instead of giving the needed context in the question.

The question is not self-contained: "all this" points back to the judgments described on earlier cards without identifying them. When those cards are no longer visible, the question does not adequately say what the LORD will do.
The question refers to "the city" without identifying it as Jerusalem. Understanding which city was breached depends on earlier cards that are no longer on screen.
"They" has no antecedent within the question. Knowing that it means Nebuzaradan and the Babylonian officials depends on story card 10, which is no longer on screen.

The question depends on card 3, which is no longer visible. "That message," "the men" and "it" do not identify the warning about going to Egypt or the leaders making the accusation, so the question is not self-contained.

The question begins, "Once the LORD saves them," but the antecedent of "them" is found only on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen. The question should identify Jacob and his descendants itself.
"In that hard line" and "who else" depend on story card 15, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to restate the first curse so that it stands on its own.

"In that day" points back to card 8 for the capture of Kirioth and the seizure of the strongholds, but that story card is no longer on screen. The question needs to carry those events itself so the baker has the context for the warriors' reaction.

The question asks about "the calamity on this nation" without identifying the nation. Its subject depends on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen, so the question does not supply its own context.

The question never identifies who “them” and “they” are. Their antecedent appears only on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible, so the question does not independently establish that it is about Babylon's people.
The question never names Jerusalem or otherwise identifies the city. Its opening "She" depends on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible.

The question refers only to "Him," relying on the preceding story card to identify the figure on the throne in Ezekiel's vision. Once that story card is off screen, the question does not supply the required context.

"Inside that hidden room" and "all those engravings" point back to cards 11-12, which are no longer on screen. The question also never names Ezekiel or freshly establishes the scene, so it is not self-contained.
The question does not identify who "they" are; that depends on remembering the preceding story card. Name the city or its people in the question itself.
"They" and "them" rely on earlier cards to identify the house of Israel. The question needs to name the house of Israel itself.
"Them" has no antecedent within the question, so the question does not identify whom God says He will gather. Name the house of Israel.
Both uses of "they" depend on earlier cards to identify who will be melted within the city. The question should name the house of Israel.
The question never identifies who "them" refers to. It depends on the earlier story card about the men portrayed on the wall, so it is not self-contained when that card is no longer visible.

"Through all of this" does not identify the judgment, and "Her" in the answers has no named antecedent in the question. The question needs to name Oholibah and give the judgment context rather than point back to earlier cards.

"God gives the reason" and "all of this" leave the events being explained unidentified without the preceding cards. The question should establish that God is explaining the judgment coming on Oholibah.

The question never identifies whose stronghold, pride and joy, and sons and daughters are meant by 'their.' The antecedent appears only on earlier cards, so the question should name Israel or the house of Israel and stand on its own.
"After that list" points back to story card 8, which is no longer on screen, without giving the baker enough context to know what list the question means.
"When it all comes to pass" depends on story card 9 for the meaning of "it all." The question does not supply that context itself, and the previous story card is no longer visible.

The question refers to "what people said" and "the land" without giving the people's accusation or identifying the land as Israel's. It relies on the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen, for that context.

The question uses "all this" to point back to the tendons, flesh, skin and breath described on story card 9. Since that card is no longer on screen, the question does not provide the needed context itself.

The question begins 'In that square inner court', using 'that' to point back to the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen. The question should supply its own context without that backward reference.

The question begins with "That gate" but never identifies the gate within the question. Its antecedent is on an earlier card, so the question does not stand on its own; it should name the inner court's east gate.
"These offerings" and "this place" have no antecedents within the question. The baker must look back to earlier cards to know which offerings and which place the statement means.
"These" has no antecedent within the question. The question should identify the four corner courts, or the courts containing the ovens, rather than relying on the preceding card.

The question relies on the previous card for its essential context: “live this way” does not explain that Nebuchadnezzar will be driven away from mankind and feed on grass like an ox. Seen on its own, the question does not say what condition Daniel is describing.

The question relies on “this” to supply the accusation from the preceding story card. By itself, it never says what Darius hears about Daniel, so the choice lacks the context needed to understand the moment.
"That king" points back to the preceding choice card for its identity. The question needs to identify him within itself, for example as the king who spoke against the Most High.
"His" and "Him" have no antecedent within the question. The question should name whose kingdom is everlasting and whom the rulers will serve and obey.

The question begins with the unidentified pronoun "He." The person taking the captives is identified only on the preceding choice card, so the question does not supply its own context when that card is no longer visible.

"Hosea asks this of his wife" does not explain what "this" means. The requirement being discussed appears only on card 9, so this question relies on a card the baker can no longer see instead of supplying its own context.

Several choice cards do not identify their subject independently. Cards 12, 15 and 17 use them or they without an antecedent; cards 13 and 14 say only the people; and card 19 depends on the phrase These are the same people. Without the earlier cards on screen, these questions do not clearly identify Ephraim or Israel.

The question relies on the previous story card for its context: “that heifer” does not identify Ephraim or explain the picture within the question itself. Make the question self-contained so it does not point back to a card the baker can no longer see.

The question begins, "Micah keeps that rough picture going," using "that" to refer back to the violent picture on story card 4, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to supply that context itself or omit the backward reference.

"Those peoples" has no antecedent within the question and points back to story card 10, which is no longer on screen. The question should identify them as the peoples Zion breaks to pieces or the nations gathered against her.
The question never identifies whose possessions are being removed. The pronouns "their" and "them" depend on "His people" in the preceding story card, which is no longer visible.

The question does not identify whose cities and strongholds these are. "Their" has no clear antecedent within the question itself and relies on context from earlier cards that the baker can no longer see.

"In this picture" depends on the preceding story card and does not identify the picture as Habakkuk's description of God measuring the earth and startling the nations. The question does not supply enough context on its own.
"All that marching" points back to the preceding story card. Standing alone, the question does not explain that the LORD marched across the earth with fury and threshed the nations in wrath.
"Those warriors" has no antecedent within the question. The card needs to identify them as the wicked one's warriors who stormed out to scatter Habakkuk's people.
"It all" leaves what Habakkuk heard undefined without the preceding story card. The question should identify the report and picture of the LORD's coming that Habakkuk has heard.
The question does not explain what event 'When this happens' refers to, and 'the one who is speaking' does not adequately identify the speaker. Both depend on cards that are no longer on screen.
The question relies on "that third" pointing back to earlier cards. Standing alone, it does not identify the group as the third left in the land.

"In that secret meeting" points back to the setup on card 13, which is no longer on screen. The question should supply the context itself, such as by saying that Herod is meeting secretly with the Magi.
"That report" points back to card 16 without explaining the report in this question. The question should say that Herod wants the Magi to report to him after they find the Child.
The question is not self-contained. "This fulfilled" points back to the preceding story card for its antecedent; the question itself never identifies what Matthew says was fulfilled.
The question depends on card 15 to explain what “it” is. Without that card on screen, the question does not identify the dispute with the adversary or the trip to court.

"Those people" has no antecedent within the question. The question needs to identify the people who will tell Jesus on that day about the works they did in His name, rather than relying on the preceding story card.
"Them" has no antecedent within the question. The people Jesus is addressing need to be identified in the question itself.

The question relies on the unidentified 'they' for who asks Jesus. The preceding story cards do not identify that group either, and they are no longer visible when the baker answers, so the question does not supply its own context.
The question ends with “upon them,” but never identifies who “them” is. The baker must rely on earlier cards to know that Jesus is addressing the Pharisees; name that audience in the question itself.
The question refers only to "they" without identifying the Pharisees and scribes, so the baker must rely on an earlier card to know whom Jesus is addressing.

The question's "this" points back to Peter's confession on the previous story card, but the question never identifies what was revealed. Since that story card is no longer on screen, the question should supply the content itself: Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God.

The phrase "in the same way" depends on the preceding story card's account of people doing whatever they wished to Elijah. The question itself never supplies that comparison, so it should restate enough of card 6 to stand on its own.

The question relies on the preceding story card: “that cup and dish” points back to context the baker can no longer see. It should itself explain that Jesus is addressing the scribes and Pharisees, who clean the outside of the cup and dish.

“That line of righteous blood” depends entirely on the preceding story card. The question should supply the needed context itself: Jesus is speaking about all the righteous blood shed on earth, extending to Zechariah.

The opening 'that servant' depends on the preceding story card to identify the faithful and wise servant. Since that card is no longer visible, the question needs to identify the servant and his assignment within its own wording.

"If the servant knew all that" relies on the preceding story card to identify which servant is meant and what "all that" refers to. The question is not self-contained once that story card is off screen.
"When he hears this" depends on Jesus' statement on the preceding story card without identifying what that statement was. The choice does not provide its own context for the high priest's reaction.

The question is not self-contained. "The man like that" depends on the previous card's description of the man as sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; on its own, the question does not identify which man or explain what "like that" means.
"Jesus takes it even further" uses "it" to point back to the preceding card's teaching rather than giving that context within the question.

The question is not self-contained. In "Once the centurion confirms it," the antecedent of "it" is that Jesus is already dead, but that appears only on earlier cards. The question should state what the centurion confirms.
The question does not identify who "the two" are or what they report with "it." Both depend on earlier cards that the baker can no longer see.
The phrase "During that famine" points back to the preceding story card for its antecedent. The question should identify the famine in Elijah's time within the question itself.

The question is not self-contained: "those tombs" and "what their fathers did" depend on earlier cards. It does not identify them as tombs for the prophets or say that the fathers killed the prophets.
The phrase "sent to them" has no antecedent within the question and relies on earlier cards to identify the recipients.
The question's "that blood" points back to earlier cards instead of identifying the blood within the question itself, such as the blood of the prophets.

"Right after that promise" points back to the preceding card without identifying the promise. The question should supply its own context by saying that Jesus has just told the disciples God will clothe them.

Cards 4 and 5 refer to "that manager," and cards 8 and 10 refer to "that servant," relying on earlier cards instead of identifying the person within the question. Cards 8 and 10 are especially unclear because they do not say that this is the servant who decided his master was delayed and began beating the other servants.

The phrase "that baptism" has no antecedent within the question and points back to story card 3, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to supply the context itself, such as identifying it as the baptism Jesus has to undergo.

The phrase "that prison" points back to the judge, officer and prison sequence on story card 19, which is no longer on screen. The choice question needs to identify the prison in its own wording rather than relying on that story card.

The question relies on card 7 to explain who 'the owners' are and what they are asking 'why' about. It should say that the colt's owners are asking why the disciples are untying it, so the question is understandable when the earlier card is no longer on screen.
'All this' points back to events described on earlier cards without saying what they are. The question needs to identify the coming destruction of Jerusalem so it stands on its own.
"To show it" makes "it" point back to card 12's statement that the dead are raised. That antecedent is not supplied in the question itself.

The question asks what “they all” ask without identifying who “they” are. The preceding story card only gives Jesus' statement, so the question depends on earlier cards that are no longer visible; it should name the council.

The question uses "them," "their presence," and "their charges" without identifying the chief priests, rulers and people. Since the setup card is no longer on screen, those pronouns lack an on-screen antecedent.
The question relies on the preceding story card to identify 'this man' as the certain Jew. Standing alone, it does not identify the other party in the dispute.
'His testimony' has no antecedent within the question. The baker must remember earlier cards to know that this means the testimony of the One from heaven.
The question does not name Jesus or identify His teaching. "His" and "it" depend on card 1, which is no longer on screen, so the question lacks the context it needs to stand alone.

The question relies on card 16's statement that Jesus called one of the Twelve a devil, but it does not restate that setup. On its own, it does not say what Jesus was speaking about, leaving the baker to depend on a card that is no longer on screen.

The question begins with “They” but never says who is trying to seize Jesus. Its antecedent is on earlier cards that are no longer visible, leaving the question without the required context about who is acting.

The phrases "all of this" and "what it means" depend on earlier cards that are no longer visible. The question does not identify Jesus' entry on the young donkey or the written words whose meaning the disciples did not yet understand.
The question's 'them' has no antecedent on the choice card. It relies on an earlier card to identify the disciples, so the question does not stand on its own when shown again for correction.
The phrase 'these things' points back to teachings on earlier cards without identifying them. The question needs to supply the context of following Jesus' example and doing what He has taught.

The phrases 'all this' and 'it' depend on the preceding cards about Jesus' chosen ones and the Scripture concerning His betrayer. Without that context, the question does not say what Jesus is telling the disciples beforehand.

The phrase "withered branches like that" points back to the description on story card 12, which is no longer on screen. Make the question self-contained by identifying which branches Jesus is describing.

The question is not self-contained. "Last on the list" depends on earlier cards and does not explain that the list is the Advocate's work of convicting the world regarding sin, righteousness and judgment.
The standalone question says “Peter denies it once more” without explaining what “it” is. It relies on the servant’s question on card 18, which is no longer on screen.

"Before that day" depends on the previous card for its meaning. The question should identify the day itself, such as the day Jesus was taken up to heaven, rather than using "that" to point back to a card the baker can no longer see.
"When the apostles ask about the timing" does not say what event's timing they are asking about. The question needs to supply the context of restoring the kingdom to Israel.
The question does not identify who "them" are. Without the preceding card, "each one of them" has no clear antecedent; the question needs to name Jesus' followers.

Several choice cards depend on context that is not stated in the question: cards 3 and 4 use “them” without identifying the crowd, card 6 refers to “this promise” without identifying it, and card 14 opens with “They're” without identifying the believers.
The phrase 'these things' points back to earlier cards without identifying what the apostles say they are witnessing about, so the question does not provide its own context.
The question never identifies 'these men' as the apostles. Its central referent depends on cards that are no longer on screen.

The opening 'it' has no antecedent within the question. It should identify the apostles' purpose or endeavor rather than relying on the previous choice card, and 'them' should likewise make clear that Gamaliel means the apostles.

The phrase "that very Scripture" points back to the earlier Isaiah cards, which are no longer on screen. The question should identify the passage itself, such as the Isaiah passage the official was reading, rather than relying on "that" for its context.

"While all this happens" depends on earlier cards without identifying what the men are reacting to. The question should briefly reestablish the light-and-voice encounter so it remains self-contained when the story card is no longer visible.
"That house" points back to story card 2, which is no longer on screen. Identify it in the question as the house of Judas on Straight Street.
The question uses “they” without identifying the people at Mary's house. That antecedent appears only on earlier cards, so the question does not fully supply its own context.

The standalone question never identifies who "they" are. With the earlier Antioch setup no longer on screen, the people who fast, pray, lay on hands and send Barnabas and Saul off lack a clear antecedent.

The question relies on “that altar,” pointing back to the inscription on the preceding story card. It should identify the altar within the question itself, such as the altar inscribed TO AN UNKNOWN GOD, so the question remains self-contained.
The question never identifies who “they” are, leaving its central pronouns dependent on cards the baker can no longer see. It should identify the listeners at the Areopagus within the question.

The standalone question does not identify the matter before Gallio. "This" and "it" point back to the accusation and legal proceeding on earlier cards that are no longer visible; the question should supply that context itself.

The phrase "beyond that" points back to the courts and complaint in the previous choice card without identifying either one. Once that card is no longer visible, the question does not supply its own context.

"After hearing all that" points back to Festus's explanation across earlier cards without saying in the question what Agrippa has heard. The question should supply that context itself, such as by referring to Festus laying out Paul's case.

The question begins by saying that Jesus says they'll turn to God without identifying who they are. The recipients, Paul's own people and the Gentiles, appear only on the preceding story card, which is no longer visible.
The question is not self-contained: "they" does not identify the people on the ship, and "that bay" points back to the preceding story card, which is no longer on screen.
The question refers to "this person," but the person who does not work but believes is identified only on the preceding story card. Restate that context so the question stands on its own.

The phrase "that timing" points back to the preceding story card without explaining the timing in the question. Either state that Abraham's faith was credited before his circumcision or remove the vague reference.
The phrase "those words" has no antecedent within the question and depends on the preceding story card. Restate the words "it was credited to him" so the baker has the necessary context on screen.
The question never identifies whose mortal bodies are meant. 'Their' and 'them' depend on the readers being identified as 'you' on earlier cards that are no longer visible.
'They' and 'them' have no antecedent within the question. The question relies on earlier cards to identify the people Paul is addressing instead of supplying that context itself.
"Paul preached that way" relies on the previous card for the meaning of "that way," so the question is not self-contained when that card is no longer visible.

"In the same way" depends on the comparison in the preceding story card, but the question does not restate that a man's own spirit knows his thoughts. Once that card is gone, the setup needed to reason out the blank is missing.
The question depends on "that lesson," pointing back to card 13 instead of giving the needed context in the question itself.
The phrase "this kind of sexual immorality" points back to card 1, which is no longer visible. The question itself does not explain that a man in the Corinthian church has his father's wife.

The question depends on "because of this" and "that home" without identifying the marriage between a believer and an unbeliever or what "this" refers to. It is not self-contained once the previous card is no longer visible.

The question begins "If that man..." but the man's situation is described only on the preceding story card. Without that card, "that man" has no antecedent; the question needs to identify him and his situation itself.
The question refers to “that food” without identifying it as food someone has said was offered to idols. It therefore relies on cards 10 and 11, which are no longer on screen, for essential context.

The question relies on "that way" to point back to the arrangement described on story card 13, but that card is no longer visible. The choice card needs to include the context itself: God giving greater honor to the parts that lacked it.
"After that quote" points back to the quotation on the preceding story card, which the baker can no longer see, without identifying the quote in the question itself.
The phrase "that crowd" points back to card 3, which is no longer on screen. The question does not identify the crowd within itself, such as the brothers who saw the risen Christ at once.
The question never identifies what 'It' is. It depends on earlier cards to establish that Paul is describing the resurrection body, so the question does not provide its own context.
The question does not identify who “them” refers to. It depends on an earlier card for the knowledge that Paul is talking about himself and the Corinthians, so it does not stand on its own.
The question never identifies whose faith and joy Paul is discussing. “Their” and “them” rely on the surrounding cards rather than naming the Corinthians in the question itself.
The question does not identify who “they'd” and “they” refer to. It needs to name the Corinthians rather than relying on the preceding story card for that context.
The question does not identify whom Satan might outwit. “Them” depends on earlier cards instead of identifying Paul and the Corinthians within the question.
The standalone question does not say who “they” are. It should identify Paul and the Corinthians rather than requiring the baker to recover the antecedent from earlier cards.

The question points back to the previous story card with "After that 'Therefore,'" even though that card is no longer on screen. Make the setup self-contained, for example by identifying the words Paul quotes and saying that the Lord speaks after "Therefore."

The choice question leaves out the setup that Paul is asking whether it was a sin to humble himself in order to exalt the Corinthians. Once the story card is gone, “What did Paul do in Corinth that he's asking the Corinthians about?” gives no basis for reasoning to preaching free of charge rather than either alternative. Include the humbling-and-exalting context in the question.
The question is not self-contained. "A man like that" points back to earlier cards without identifying the man as the one who was caught up to the third heaven and Paradise.

The question refers to what Cephas and the other Jews are doing without identifying that action. The choice card does not explain that they have drawn back and separated themselves from the Gentiles, so it depends on the baker remembering earlier cards.
"Stays out of it" uses "it" to point back to the withdrawal and hypocrisy described on earlier cards. The question never says what Barnabas is supposedly staying out of.
"That harvest" points back to the preceding choice card instead of identifying the harvest within this question, so the statement is not self-contained.

The question relies on "this purpose" without identifying the purpose in the question itself. Since the preceding story card is no longer visible, it should identify the purpose God accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord.

The question names only Paul and then uses "them" and "their" without identifying the believers. It should say that Paul's sufferings for the believers are their glory so the question remains self-contained.

Several choice questions rely on context that is no longer on screen. In stop 1, cards 5, 10 and 13 use 'they' or 'their' without identifying the Gentiles or believers, and card 7 refers to 'this way of living' without identifying the Gentiles' way of life. In stop 2, cards 14 and 17 likewise use 'they' without naming Paul's audience. Each question should supply its own antecedents and context.
The question says “their growing love” and “helps them” without identifying whose love it is. The preceding story card is no longer visible, so the question needs to name the believers at Philippi.
The question relies on the earlier Timothy cards to explain who 'all the others' are. On its own, it never says that they are the others besides Timothy, so it does not provide sufficient context.
The question never identifies the Philippians as the people who will see Epaphroditus again. It calls them only 'they,' leaving that pronoun without an antecedent in the question.
"These people's" has no antecedent within the question. The baker must rely on cards that are no longer visible to know that Paul is describing the enemies of the cross.
The question depends on card 16 for the identity of "these" and "they." Once that card is off screen, the question does not identify the regulations or prohibitions whose basis it asks about.

"These restrictions" points back to card 18 without identifying which restrictions Paul means. The question needs its own context, such as the restrictions involving self-prescribed worship, false humility and harsh treatment of the body.

The question depends on “those ways” without identifying which ways Paul means. The preceding story card is about God's wrath and does not identify them either, so the baker must reconstruct the question's meaning from earlier cards that are no longer on screen.
The question never identifies whose spirit, soul and body Paul means. The pronoun "their" depends on earlier cards that are no longer on screen, so the question does not provide its own context.
"Will do it" has no antecedent within the question. Understanding what "it" means requires remembering the sanctification and preservation described on earlier cards.
"All this" points back to the repayment and relief described on earlier cards without identifying what will take place, so the question does not supply its own context.
The question refers to “that city” without naming Ephesus. Its referent appears only on earlier cards, so the question does not fully supply its own context.

The question relies on "that prayer list" from an earlier card instead of restating the needed context, such as Paul's call to pray for everyone. It is not fully self-contained when the earlier card is no longer visible.

“Him” and “the list” have no antecedent within the question and depend on remembering earlier cards. The question should identify whose confession or list it is, such as the One who appeared in the flesh, so it stands alone.

"Some of them" has no antecedent within the question. The group, those under the yoke of slavery, is identified only on earlier cards, so the question needs to name them rather than rely on a pronoun pointing backward.
The phrase "men like that" depends on the preceding story card for its antecedent. The question never identifies the men or their irreverent, empty chatter, so it is not self-contained.
The question relies on "the seal" and "the second saying" without identifying the seal on God's firm foundation. That context exists only on earlier cards, which the baker can no longer see.
"People who gather teachers like that" makes "that" point back to earlier cards. The question needs to supply the context itself by saying that they gather teachers to suit their own desires.
The question is not self-contained. "That prophet" and "the saying" point back to card 5 without identifying the Cretan prophet or what he said.
The question depends on earlier cards to identify "that prophet's testimony." It needs to identify the Cretan prophet's testimony within the question itself.
"Them" has no antecedent within the question. The question needs to say that Titus is to rebuke the false teachers rather than relying on earlier cards.
"Them" has no antecedent within the question, so it does not identify whose attention Paul is discussing. The people being rebuked need to be identified in the question.
"These men" points back to earlier cards without identifying the men. The question should identify them as the men who profess to know God but deny Him by their actions.
The question does not stand alone: 'if Titus teaches this way' points back to the previous story card without identifying the integrity, dignity and wholesome speech that it described.
The question does not stand alone: 'If slaves live this way' points back to instructions on earlier cards without saying which way of life it means.
The question is not self-contained. "That rest" points back to earlier cards instead of identifying God's rest in the question itself.
The question points back to the previous card with "that one man" instead of identifying Abraham, so it does not supply its own context.

The question begins with "That man," but the man is identified only on story card 15, which is no longer on screen. The question needs to identify him as the person who considers himself religious yet does not bridle his tongue.
The question uses "they" without identifying the planners, so it depends on the previous story card for its meaning. The question itself should name the planners.
"All such boasting" has no referent within the question and points back to the previous card's mention of the planners' proud intentions. The question should identify that boasting itself.
The question depends on the previous card to identify who 'them' and 'they' are. On its own, it never identifies the people Christ suffered for, so it lacks the required context.

The question relies on "this way" without saying what that means. The card does not itself explain that believers are to speak as one conveying God's words and serve with the strength God provides, so it depends on context from earlier cards that are no longer on screen.

The pronoun "them" depends on earlier cards to identify Peter's audience. When this question appears by itself, it does not say who Peter is addressing; identify them as the believers in the question.
The pronoun "they" has no antecedent within the question and relies on earlier cards to identify Peter's readers. Make the question self-contained by naming the believers or using "a believer."

Several choice cards rely on the preceding cards to identify their subject. Cards 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12 and 17 use "these men" or bare pronouns without identifying the false teachers, so the questions do not consistently stand alone when the story card is no longer visible.

Cards 2 and 4 do not identify who "they" or "these men" are. Card 10 also depends on "those two proverbs" and "these people" without identifying the proverbs or the people, although the preceding story card containing them is no longer visible.
The question relies on "them" and "this" from earlier cards instead of identifying the recipients and subject. It should stand alone, for example by naming the believers and the Lord's patience.

Many choice questions rely on antecedents or context absent from the question itself: stop 1 cards 14 and 15 use He and Him without naming Jesus, and card 17 refers to this new voice; stop 2 card 2 refers to all this, card 12 uses His with John as the nearest named person, card 13 refers to all of this, and cards 15 through 18 repeatedly use He or His without identifying the speaker. The baker has to reconstruct the subject from cards that are no longer visible.
The question never identifies who is singing. "Their" and "they" depend on earlier cards that are no longer on screen; the question should identify the living creatures and elders as the singers.
The question is not self-contained. "There" points back to card 2's answer without naming what John is measuring, so the necessary context disappears with the earlier card.

The question depends on "all of this" pointing back to the preceding story card. Without that card, it does not identify what has come: the salvation, power and kingdom of God, and the authority of His Christ.
The question says "her immorality" without identifying the woman. Its antecedent is only on earlier cards, so the question does not stand on its own.
The question refers to "the name on her forehead" without saying whose forehead or which name. It relies on earlier cards for its basic context.
The phrase "that war" points back to earlier cards instead of identifying the war within the question.
The phrases "their hearts" and "their kingdom" have no antecedent in the question. It never identifies these people as the ten kings.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

examples: Cards 8-9 cover the skies pouring down righteousness and imply that the earth opens, but never say that salvation may sprout and righteousness spring up with it, or that the LORD has created it. This leaves out the central result of Isaiah 45:8.

The only treatment of who sees God's salvation is a false statement saying it will be seen by Zion alone. Marking that false establishes only that the scope is wider than Zion; neither this card nor card 9 tells the central facts that the LORD bares His arm in the sight of all nations and that all the ends of the earth will see His salvation (Isaiah 52:10).

The stop ends without ever mentioning the LORD's promise in Isaiah 54:10 that His covenant of peace will not be broken. Card 19 covers His loving devotion, but the unbroken covenant of peace is another central promise in that verse.

places.problem: Cards 8-9 cover the skies pouring down righteousness and imply that the earth opens, but never say that salvation may sprout and righteousness spring up with it, or that the LORD has created it. This leaves out the central result of Isaiah 45:8.

The only treatment of who sees God's salvation is a false statement saying it will be seen by Zion alone. Marking that false establishes only that the scope is wider than Zion; neither this card nor card 9 tells the central facts that the LORD bares His arm in the sight of all nations and that all the ends of the earth will see His salvation (Isaiah 52:10).

The stop ends without ever mentioning the LORD's promise in Isaiah 54:10 that His covenant of peace will not be broken. Card 19 covers His loving devotion, but the unbroken covenant of peace is another central promise in that verse.

The only treatment of the second half of verse 11 is the false statement that the Savior comes empty-handed. No card tells the baker that His reward is with Him and His recompense goes before Him, leaving an important part of the proclamation untaught.

The closing question elicits only "Sought Out," and no card mentions the verse's other name, "A City Not Forsaken." The walkthrough ends without teaching the full closing promise and its bookend to Zion's old name.

The only treatment of the last part of verse 20 is a false statement saying the person will be considered blessed. Marking it false establishes only that the person is not blessed; no card ever tells the baker that the verse says such a person will be considered accursed.

Verse 10 is reduced to an unnamed job list. Neither this card nor card 17 supplies the list, so the baker misses uprooting, tearing down, destroying and overthrowing, followed by building and planting. The true-or-false question only establishes that the work is not exclusively destructive.

No card mentions that the people also poured out drink offerings to other gods on these rooftops. Since this card asks what the people did there, covering only the incense leaves out part of the very conduct for which the houses would be defiled in verse 13.

The walkthrough covers the call to turn from wickedness but never includes the LORD's promise in verse 3 to forgive their iniquity and sin. That promise is a central part of why the scroll is written, and no later card supplies it.

Marking this statement false only tells the baker that Jehoiakim will not receive the described honorable burial. No card teaches the verse's actual judgment: his body will be thrown out and exposed to heat by day and frost by night.

The walkthrough ends by asking only whom the LORD will pursue. No card tells the rest of Lamentations 3:66, that He will exterminate them from under His heavens, omitting an important part of the passage's climax.

The fourth case never covers the final result in verse 21: when the righteous man heeds the warning and lives, Ezekiel also saves himself. Cards 10 and 11 cover only the righteous man's response and life, leaving out the watchman's repeated outcome, an important part of the four-case teaching.

The card reduces verse 13 to eating defiled bread among the nations, and no other card says that these are nations to which God will banish the Israelites. That leaves out an important part of the sign's meaning: the coming banishment is something God says He will do.

The walkthrough never covers the final words of verse 17, "in their iniquity." Card 14 mentions only the lack of food and water, and this card asks only about the people wasting away, so the passage's final connection between their wasting away and their iniquity is lost.

The walkthrough leaves out an important part of Ezekiel 14:11: the house of Israel will no longer defile themselves with all their transgressions. Card 13 covers no longer straying from God, and card 14 moves directly to Israel being His people and God being their God, so this part of the LORD's stated purpose is never told or asked.

Ezekiel 47:22 specifically describes foreigners who dwell among Israel and have children. Card 7's answer omits that qualification, and card 8 then describes the foreigners simply as those who live among Israel. The walkthrough never teaches this part of the verse, making residence alone sound like the qualification for the inheritance.

Verse 10 also says that, despite all this, Israel does not seek the LORD. No card tells or asks about that concluding indictment; the false answer here only establishes that Israel does not return to Him.

The stop moves straight to the LORD's roar and never tells verse 10's opening statement that they will walk after the LORD. That omits the important reversal from turning away from Him to following Him.

The correct answer covers only the first part of Joel 1:3. No card includes the children telling their children, and their children telling the next generation, so the verse's important command to pass the account down through successive generations is lost.

Joel 2:23 says that the autumn rains are given 'for your vindication,' but neither card covering that verse mentions this purpose. The stop covers the rains themselves while leaving out an important part of God's promise.

The retelling of Joel 3:3 says only that they bartered a boy away, leaving out that they bartered him for a prostitute. That specific charge is an important part of the nations' exploitation of the LORD's people and helps explain the judgment announced in the passage.

This card uses only the first half of Joel 3:20. Nothing in the walkthrough tells the baker that Jerusalem will continue from generation to generation, so the closing promise concerning Jerusalem is dropped.

The decisive turn in Amos 7:8 is left unclear. Marking this compound statement false does not establish whether Amos does not plead again, whether the LORD does not relent, or both. No other card clearly tells the Lord's actual announcement that He will no longer spare Israel.

This is the only card for Micah 4:5, and rejecting its distorted statement does not tell the baker what the verse actually affirms. The walkthrough moves straight to 4:6 without ever giving the central contrast: though the nations may walk in the names of their gods, Micah's side will walk in the name of the LORD their God forever and ever.

Two important positive facts are never actually taught. Stop 1 card 11 only lets the baker reject keeping the wealth; no card says Zion devotes the gain to the LORD and the wealth to the Lord of all the earth (Micah 4:13). Stop 2 card 7 only rejects shepherding in His own strength; no card says He shepherds in the strength of the LORD and in the majestic name of the LORD His God (Micah 5:4).

The actual outcome in the second half of Micah 5:9 is omitted. Choosing False establishes only that the enemies will not make peace; neither this card nor a later card tells the baker that all the enemies will be cut off.

The resolution of verse 9 is never told. This card stops at Micah enduring the LORD's rage, and card 5 covers only God arguing his case; no card says that God executes justice for him, brings him into the light, or lets him see His righteousness. That leaves an important turn in the passage uncovered.

The important statement in Haggai 2:14 that every work of the people's hands is defiled is never clearly communicated. This card quotes only the people-and-nation clause before moving into its joke, and card 9 asks only about their offerings. The later statement that their work was struck with blight, mildew and hail does not supply the missing detail that their work was defiled.

The card substitutes the kings of Judah for the actual promise, but no card ever tells the baker that Joshua is promised a place among these who are standing here (Zechariah 3:7). Choosing False only rejects the substitute and leaves that part of the verse untaught.

Cards 12-13 cover the lack of compassion and falling into the hands of a neighbor and king, but omit the rest of verse 6: those hands will devastate the land, and the LORD will not deliver it. These concluding judgments are not covered anywhere else.
The walkthrough stops verse 9 after the dying die and the perishing perish. It never covers the verse's concluding judgment that those who remain will devour one another's flesh.

Marking the marketplace statement false only tells the baker where the silver was not thrown. No card states verse 13's actual location: the prophet threw the silver to the potter in the house of the LORD.

Marking this statement false only establishes that John's disciples did not go and tell Herod. No card states what Matthew 14:12 actually says next: they went and informed Jesus. The passage's final action is therefore left untaught.
The walkthrough never identifies the one Instructor as "the Christ." Correctly marking this statement False only rejects Moses, so the key identification in verse 10 remains untold.

The question asks where else people are coming from, but the correct answer omits the region beyond the Jordan from Mark 3:8. No later card covers it, so the walkthrough leaves the list of places incomplete.

The walkthrough covers whom the unforgivable blasphemy is against and that it will never be forgiven, but no card covers the rest of Mark 3:29: "he is guilty of eternal sin." This leaves out a key part of Jesus' warning.

This is the only treatment of Jesus sending the Twelve two by two. Because the statement is false, the baker learns only that they were not sent out one at a time; no card ever supplies the actual detail that Jesus sent them in pairs.
Only the first half of Mark 10:31 is covered. The cards teach that many who are first will be last, but never tell or ask Jesus' concluding statement that the last will be first.

The walkthrough never supplies Gabriel's actual time limit for Zechariah's silence. Card 12 says only that he will be unable to speak, and this card rules out leaving the temple without teaching that the silence lasts until the day the promise comes to pass (Luke 1:20), an important detail of the sign.

The walkthrough never tells or asks the first part of verse 39: after drinking old wine, the person does not want the new. Card 8 covers only the concluding statement that the old is better, leaving out the rejection of the new, an important part of Jesus' final picture.

No card states that Jesus says the great reward is in heaven. This card only rejects the idea of a reward on earth, and card 8 moves straight to the prophets, leaving out an important part of verse 23 and the reason Jesus gives for rejoicing.
Luke 9:31 also says that Moses and Elijah appeared in glory, but no card tells that detail. Card 5 covers only their topic of conversation, leaving out a significant part of their appearance.

The walkthrough never tells the baker that Jesus turned and rebuked James and John in Luke 9:55. Marking the statement that Jesus told them to go ahead as false only establishes what He did not do, leaving an important detail of the passage untold.

The stop never conveys that the one who seeks finds (Luke 11:9-10). Card 2 names seeking, and cards 2-3 cover the promises connected with knocking and asking, but no story or choice card gives the promise connected with seeking, leaving out part of Jesus' threefold teaching.

Verse 44 is reduced to a false statement about leaving the walls standing. The walkthrough never clearly tells that the enemies will level Jerusalem and the children within its walls, or that they will not leave one stone on another. Those are central details of Jesus's warning, not minor details that can be dropped.

Neither this question nor the earlier cards clearly state Luke 20:33's key premise that all seven brothers were married to the woman. Card 6 mentions the second and third marriages and then says only that all seven died, leaving out an important part of what makes the Sadducees' riddle work.

Luke 21:34 names dissipation, drunkenness, and the worries of life, but the stop never mentions dissipation or drunkenness. Its only question about the list asks solely for the worries of life, leaving out two important dangers in Jesus' warning.

Luke 22:18 appears only as an invented statement to reject. The walkthrough never clearly tells the baker what Jesus actually says: He will not drink of the fruit of the vine from now on until the kingdom of God comes. Marking the statement false does not convey that positive statement or its kingdom timing.

The stop never includes Philip's statement in John 1:45 that Jesus is the One the prophets foretold. It covers Moses and the Law, then moves directly to Jesus of Nazareth and Joseph, leaving out an important part of Philip's announcement.
The right answer covers only doing the will of the One who sent Jesus. John 4:34 also makes finishing His work part of Jesus's food, and no other card includes that part of His explanation.

Neither the setup nor the answer includes the people's claim that when the Christ comes, no one will know where He is from. Without that part of verse 27, simply knowing where Jesus is from does not explain their doubt, so the passage's reasoning is lost.

The walkthrough leaves out the second half of Jesus' promise in John 8:12: His followers will have the light of life. Card 1 quotes only His opening claim, and this card's correct answer stops at never walking in darkness, so a central detail of the passage is never covered.

This card asks only about Jesus's hypothetical statement that He would be a liar. Neither this card nor any other covers John 8:55's main contrast: the crowd does not know the Father, while Jesus knows Him and keeps His word. That leaves an important part of Jesus's answer untold.

The walkthrough never conveys the second half of Jesus's answer in John 11:4: the sickness is also so that the Son of God may be glorified through it. That purpose is an important detail, not merely omitted wording.

The correct answer stops at telling the people, and no later card supplies what they are to proclaim: the full message of this new life. This leaves out the content and purpose of the angel's command in Acts 5:20.

The only card covering Acts 13:47 asks about being made "A light for the Gentiles" but drops the stated purpose, "to bring salvation to the ends of the earth." No later card supplies it, leaving out the global salvation purpose central to Paul's explanation of the turn to the Gentiles.

The false statement only establishes that danger can also arise from the elders' own number. No card teaches the rest of Acts 20:30: these men will distort the truth to draw disciples away after them. That is an important part of Paul's warning, not merely incidental wording.

Acts 22:16 is used only for a false statement about delaying baptism. The walkthrough never tells Ananias's actual instruction to get up, be baptized, wash Paul's sins away and call on His name, leaving out an important part of the sermon.

Answering False only establishes that peace is not the outcome for the self-seeking. No card supplies Paul's actual statement in verse 8 that there will be wrath and anger for those who reject the truth and follow wickedness, leaving an important outcome untaught.

Romans 4:17 gives two descriptions of God, but the walkthrough covers only His giving life to the dead. No card mentions that He calls into being what does not yet exist, leaving out a distinct and important part of Paul's description.

The treatment of Romans 8:20 omits an important part of the verse: creation was subjected not only apart from its own will, but because of the One who subjected it. Cards 5 and 6 establish the futility and negate creation's own will, but no card supplies the positive agent, leaving the account of the subjection incomplete.

The card covers Israel's disobedience and its purpose of mercy, but leaves out that Israel may receive this mercy through the mercy shown to the Gentiles. No other card supplies that part of Romans 11:31, so the reciprocal movement of mercy in the passage is incomplete.

The correct answer and surrounding cards reduce the end of Romans 12:2 to God's will and never mention that Paul describes it as good, pleasing and perfect. That description is an important part of what the renewed mind enables the believers to test and approve.

The walkthrough never conveys Paul's positive purpose in Romans 15:2: pleasing one's neighbor is 'for his good, to build him up.' Rejecting 'just to keep him off your back' only rules out a selfish motive and leaves this important detail untaught.

No card states that believers overflow with hope 'by the power of the Holy Spirit.' Marking 'by their own strength' false rules out one source but never teaches the source Paul actually names, leaving out a central detail of Romans 15:13.

Verse 11 says the Corinthians were washed, sanctified and justified, but the walkthrough only says they were washed and made right with God. Neither this card nor any other conveys that they were sanctified, leaving out part of Paul's concluding transformation.

This card covers only the two cups from verse 21. No card tells the verse's parallel warning that the Corinthians cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too, leaving part of Paul's concluding warning untold.

The only card covering verse 7 leaves out its closing qualification, "if the Lord permits," and no later card covers it. The walkthrough therefore misses an important qualification on Paul's hope for a longer visit.

The positive content of verse 6 is never fully covered. This false statement only rules out Jerusalem, and no card explains that Paul's affliction is for the Corinthians' comfort and salvation. In particular, the important detail of their salvation is omitted entirely.

The correct answer drops an important part of Paul's stated purpose. In 7:12, the Corinthians' earnestness was to be made clear "to you" in the sight of God. Saying only that it "would be clear before God" loses the recipient and can sound as though the purpose was for God to see their earnestness.

The retelling of 8:19 stops at administering the offering to honor the Lord and omits the other stated purpose: to show Paul's team's eagerness to help. No later card covers that purpose, leaving out one of the verse's two parallel purposes.

The correct answer includes only the proof of the Corinthians' love. In 8:24, Paul also tells them to show the reason for his team's boasting about them, and no card includes that as part of what the Corinthians are to show.

The walkthrough never says that the Lord gave Paul authority for building the Corinthians up. Card 13 only rules out tearing them down, and this card refers vaguely to "that authority," leaving out a key part of verse 8.

Verse 11's detail about Paul's large letters is never actually taught. Card 1 mentions only that Paul writes with his own hand, and marking the statement about tiny handwriting as False does not establish that Paul calls attention to his large letters. No later card supplies that detail.

The coverage of Ephesians 3:7 never includes that the gift of God's grace was given to Paul through the working of God's power. Cards 1 and 2 cover Paul's servanthood and God's grace, but this part of the verse disappears.

Ephesians 3:11 calls this God's eternal purpose, but neither this card nor the preceding story card says that it is eternal. Marking "a brand new plan God came up with recently" false only establishes that it is not recent and leaves the verse's key description unstated.

Verse 6's “until the day of Christ Jesus” is never conveyed. Card 17's later mention of the day of Christ concerns being pure and blameless, not the completion of God's good work, so an important qualifier from verse 6 is missing.

The walkthrough never positively states that the fruit of righteousness comes through Jesus Christ. Marking “their own hard work” false only rules out one possible source; it does not teach the actual source given in verse 11.

The walkthrough's treatment of verse 28 stops with the sign of the opponents' destruction and the Philippians' salvation. Neither this card nor any other includes the verse's concluding statement that it is from God, leaving out an important part of Paul's message.

The walkthrough never teaches the key positive fact of Colossians 1:12: the Father has qualified the Colossians to share in the inheritance. Card 9 only says they get a share, and marking this statement False merely denies self-qualification without ever identifying the Father's qualifying action.

The correct answer mentions power and the Holy Spirit but omits the great conviction that 1 Thessalonians 1:5 also describes. No other card covers it, leaving out part of Paul's explanation of how the gospel came to them.

Verse 16's movements “was proclaimed among the nations” and “was believed in throughout the world” are never told or positively asked. Learning only that the news was not a secret shared by a few does not give the baker those two important parts of the confession.

The answer stops at obtaining salvation, and no other card explains that this salvation is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory. In particular, the unique eternal-glory promise in verse 10 is left untaught.

Verse 14's actual consequence is never told. Marking this statement False only establishes that quarreling over words does not sharpen listeners; no card says that it leads the listeners to ruin, an important detail of the verse.

The treatment of verse 24 covers only not being quarrelsome and being kind to everyone. Being able to teach and being forbearing are never told anywhere, leaving important parts of Paul's description of the Lord's servant missing.
The answer stops at repentance, and no other card explains that the repentance Paul hopes for leads to a knowledge of the truth. That outcome from verse 25 is therefore missing.
No card covers verse 2's "with every form of patient instruction," leaving out how Timothy is to reprove, rebuke and encourage.

The stop never conveys that anyone who opposes them 'will be ashamed' in Titus 2:8. This card only asks the baker to reject the claim about having plenty of bad things to say, leaving out that part of Paul's stated result.

No card includes the last sentence of Titus 3:8, that these things are excellent and profitable for the people. That leaves out an important part of Paul's movement from devotion to good deeds in verse 8 to the pointless and worthless things in verse 9.

The sign-off covers the greetings from Paul's companions and the final blessing, but it omits Paul's separate instruction in Titus 3:15 to greet those who love them in the faith. That instruction is not covered anywhere else.

The false statement only establishes that receiving Onesimus as a stranger is not Paul's instruction. No card states the actual request in verse 17: Philemon is to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul. This leaves out a central detail of Paul's appeal.

Hebrews 1:8 says that the Son's throne endures forever and ever, but no card states that fact. Marking "only for a season" false merely rejects one invented duration and leaves this important description of the Son's throne untaught.

Hebrews 2:4 says that the gifts of the Holy Spirit were distributed according to God's will, but no card teaches that positive detail. Marking "whoever asked first" false only rules out one invented method, and the walkthrough ends without covering the last part of the verse.

Verse 20's first half is never actually taught: Peter asks what credit there is in being beaten for doing wrong and enduring it. Card 5 only says that two people suffer, and card 6 covers the doing-good case, leaving the central contrast incomplete.

No card clearly states that Jesus did not retaliate when abuse was heaped on Him. This combined true/false statement can be false merely because He made no threats, which card 12 then states, so the non-retaliation part of verse 23 is left untaught.
The answer stops with the morning star rising, and no card includes the important detail that it rises "in your hearts" from 2 Peter 1:19. That part of the verse is therefore never taught.

Marking this statement false establishes only that the sacrifice is not restricted to the letter's original readers. No card ever tells the baker that 1 John 2:2 explicitly includes “the sins of the whole world,” leaving the passage's final and important scope unstated.

The walkthrough never includes the rest of 2 John 1:4: the children were walking in the truth 'just as the Father has commanded us.' Neither this card nor the following choice card conveys that their walk was obedience to the Father's command, an important connection to the commandments discussed in verses 5-6.

Two important parts of the passage are only approached through negation and are never actually taught. Stop 1 card 5 can be answered false without the baker learning that verse 3 also blesses those who hear and obey. Stop 2 card 17 can be answered false without presenting verse 19's three-part command; in particular, the things that are never appear on any card.

The walkthrough only says that fire comes out of the witnesses' mouths. It never conveys the rest of verse 5: the fire devours their enemies, and anyone who wants to harm them must be killed. That lethal protection is an important detail, especially before the beast is later able to kill them.

The only card covering Revelation 18:24 gives an incomplete answer to What is it? It names the blood of prophets and saints but omits the blood of all who had been slain on the earth. No other card teaches that final, sweeping part of the indictment against Babylon.

rule.text: Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

examples: The card cites only Isaiah 49:18, but it also retells Zion's complaint from Isaiah 49:14 when it says that she said she had been forgotten. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card retells the mute watchdogs of Isaiah 56:10 and identifies the shepherds of Isaiah 56:11 before moving to Isaiah 56:12, but it cites only Isaiah 56:12. Its citation should span Isaiah 56:10-12.
The opening clause, 'Peace to those far and near,' tells Isaiah 57:19, but the card cites only Isaiah 57:20. Its citation should be Isaiah 57:19-20.

places.problem: The card cites only Isaiah 49:18, but it also retells Zion's complaint from Isaiah 49:14 when it says that she said she had been forgotten. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card retells the mute watchdogs of Isaiah 56:10 and identifies the shepherds of Isaiah 56:11 before moving to Isaiah 56:12, but it cites only Isaiah 56:12. Its citation should span Isaiah 56:10-12.
The opening clause, 'Peace to those far and near,' tells Isaiah 57:19, but the card cites only Isaiah 57:20. Its citation should be Isaiah 57:19-20.
The card tells Jeremiah 9:8 but also retells the earlier image of tongues bent like bows from Jeremiah 9:3. Citing only Jeremiah 9:8 is narrower than the verses the card uses.

The card retells the gentle-lamb image from Jeremiah 11:19, but its citation is only Jeremiah 12:3-4 and it gives no reference for 11:19. The citation therefore does not cover everything the card tells.
The card explicitly uses the lion from verse 8 and the bird from verse 9 alongside the vineyard from verse 10, but it cites only Jeremiah 12:10. The citation should cover Jeremiah 12:8-10.
The description "the man who put the prophet in the stocks" uses the action from verse 2, but the card cites only verse 6. The citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card places Shemaiah among the exiles in Babylon, but Jeremiah 29:24-25 does not state that detail. It is supported later in the passage, so the cited range does not cover everything the card tells.

The last sentence says that the word starts with a job for Jeremiah, which uses Jeremiah 30:2, but the card cites only Jeremiah 30:1. The citation should extend through the verse that mentions the job.

The second sentence moves into Jeremiah 31:1 by saying that the LORD then speaks about what will be true at that time, but the card cites only Jeremiah 30:24. Its citation should include every verse it uses.
The teaser about something that 'shows up on time, every time' draws on the appointed day-and-night cycle in verse 20, but the card cites only verse 19.
The statement that Babylon's army had surrounded Jerusalem uses Jeremiah 37:5, but the card cites only Jeremiah 37:19-20. Its citation does not cover every Bible fact it tells.
"The walls are open" retells the breach from Jeremiah 39:2, but the card cites only Jeremiah 39:3. The citation is too narrow for everything the card tells.
By saying that the LORD speaks "again" and that the command occurs "Twice in a row," the card uses both Jeremiah 46:27 and Jeremiah 46:28, but it cites only Jeremiah 46:28.
The card tells verse 4, but its second sentence also uses verse 5 when it says that the LORD then says something about Israel and Judah. The citation therefore ends one verse too early.
The second sentence retells Ezekiel 21:20 by identifying Rabbah as the city at the end of the other road, but the card cites only Ezekiel 21:28.

The closing sentence retells the earlier appearances of Assyria, Elam, Meshech and Tubal, Edom, and Sidon, beginning in Ezekiel 32:22, but the card cites only Ezekiel 32:32. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.
The second sentence retells Hosea 11:1 by saying Egypt is the place the LORD called Israel out of, but the card's citation covers only Hosea 11:5.
The closing clause about the prophet reaching out to the LORD retells Joel's call in Joel 1:19, but the card cites only Joel 1:20. The citation is too narrow for everything the card uses.

The card cites only Jonah 2:7, but its second sentence also retells Jonah 2:4 when it says Jonah had said he would look toward God's temple once more. The citation is narrower than the verses the card uses; following the first-to-last rule, it would be Jonah 2:4-7.

The opening sentence reuses the net from Micah 7:2, the bribe from Micah 7:3 and the thorn from Micah 7:4 before turning to Micah 7:7. Citing only Micah 7:7 leaves out the earlier verses the card uses.
The card says that the LORD's next word through Haggai is a question, which uses Haggai 1:4, but its citation stops at Haggai 1:3. The citation needs to extend through Haggai 1:4.
The card retells the four horns scattering God's people from Zechariah 1:19, but its verses field cites only Zechariah 1:20. The citation should cover Zechariah 1:19-20.

The card cites only Zechariah 9:17, but its opening sentence also retells the waterless pit from Zechariah 9:11 and the jewels in a crown from Zechariah 9:16. Its citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The card retells the Magi asking where the King of the Jews is, which comes from Matthew 2:2, as well as Herod hearing the news in 2:3. Citing only Matthew 2:3 is too narrow; the card uses Matthew 2:2-3.
Identifying these as the prophet's words uses Matthew 2:5, while the quoted prophecy comes from 2:6. The citation of only Matthew 2:6 is too narrow; the card uses Matthew 2:5-6.
The statement that the man came in lying on a mat retells Matthew 9:2, but the card cites only Matthew 9:7. Its citation therefore does not cover every passage verse the card uses.

The card cites only Matthew 13:8, but its opening also retells the path, rocky ground and thorns and their unsuccessful results from Matthew 13:4-7. Its citation does not begin with the earliest verse the card uses.

The card retells that the crowd knows Jesus's mother and brothers, which comes from Matthew 13:55, as well as the sisters and repeated question in verse 56. Citing only Matthew 13:56 is too narrow for the material the card uses.
The sentence "She came in asking about seats" retells the mother's request from Matthew 20:21, but the card cites only Matthew 20:22. Its citation should begin with the first verse it uses.
"The sea goes quiet" retells the calm from Mark 4:39, but the card cites only Mark 4:40. Its citation does not begin with the first verse it uses.
The flat, calm sea retells Mark 4:39, while the disciples' fearful question comes from Mark 4:41. Citing only Mark 4:41 omits the earlier verse the card uses.

The opening clause retells Jesus taking the little girl by the hand and her getting up, which is Mark 5:41-42, but the card cites only Mark 6:5. Its citation is narrower than the Bible content it tells.

The card retells Jesus' warning about leaven from Mark 8:15 before covering the disciples' discussion and Jesus' questions in Mark 8:16-17. Its citation starts at Mark 8:16 instead of the first verse it uses, so the range should be Mark 8:15-17.

The opening sentence retells the darkened sun and moon and the falling stars from Mark 13:24-25 before introducing verse 26, but the card cites only Mark 13:26. Its used range is Mark 13:24-26, unless the retelling is removed.
The card uses the rebuke from Mark 16:14 as well as the mission in Mark 16:15, but it cites only Mark 16:15.
The closing sentence retells the Eleven's earlier unbelief from Mark 16:14, but the card cites only Mark 16:20. The citation does not cover all the passage facts the card uses.
The card tells Luke 4:29 but also states that this crowd had spoken well of Jesus, which uses Luke 4:22. Its citation of only Luke 4:29 does not cover everything the card uses.
The sentence “He came in through the ROOF” retells Luke 5:19, but the card cites only Luke 5:25. The citation does not include the first verse the card uses.
The closing joke retells the lowering through the tiles in Luke 5:19 and the man going home in Luke 5:25, but the card cites only Luke 5:26.
The card cites only Luke 8:12 but also tells that the birds got the seed along the path, a detail from Luke 8:5. Its citation does not cover everything the card uses.
The card cites only Luke 8:48, but its last sentence also retells Luke 8:43 with “Twelve years of physicians and empty pockets.” The citation does not cover all the passage verses the card uses.

The opening sentence retells Luke 10:28 when it says Jesus just told the expert he was right, before the card moves to Luke 10:29. Citing only Luke 10:29 is too narrow; the card should cite Luke 10:28-29 or remove the recap.

The card retells the expert's neighbor question from Luke 10:29 and his original test of Jesus from Luke 10:25, as well as quoting Luke 10:37. Its citation of only Luke 10:37 does not cover what the card tells.
The setup about people accusing Jesus of driving out demons by Beelzebul retells Luke 11:15, but the card cites only Luke 11:27.
