The joke explicitly retells the mute man speaking from Luke 11:14, but the card cites only Luke 11:29.
The statement that Nineveh will condemn this generation "too," followed by "First a queen," also uses the Queen of the South's condemnation from Luke 11:31, but the card cites only Luke 11:32.
The comparison "just like with Solomon" uses the statement about Solomon from Luke 11:31, but the card's passage citation covers only Luke 11:32.
"He planned for many years" draws on Luke 12:19, while "You fool!" and "this very night" come from Luke 12:20. Citing only Luke 12:20 is too narrow; the card should cite Luke 12:19-20.

The card uses the burning lamps from Luke 12:35 as well as the master's return and the servants being found on watch in Luke 12:37, but it cites only Luke 12:37. The citation is narrower than the verses the card tells.
The phrase "Straight off the field" retells the servant coming in from the field in Luke 17:7, but the card's citation begins at Luke 17:8. Its range should begin with the first verse it uses.
The first sentence retells the leaders' demand for silence from Luke 18:39, while the second uses Luke 18:40. Citing only Luke 18:40 is too narrow; the card uses Luke 18:39-40.

The card retells Jesus driving out the sellers, which comes from Luke 19:45, as well as His declaration in Luke 19:46. Its citation covers only Luke 19:46, so it is narrower than the verses the card uses.

The card cites only Luke 21:29, but its joke also uses the detail that the trees sprout leaves, "when those leaves pop out," which comes from Luke 21:30. The story card's citation is therefore narrower than the verses it uses.
The opening sentence retells the arrangement of one criminal on each side of Jesus, which comes from Luke 23:33, but the card cites only Luke 23:39.
The card cites only Luke 24:31, but the detail that Jesus had been reclining comes from Luke 24:30. The citation should be Luke 24:30-31, or the reclining detail should be removed.
The card cites only John 1:18, but its closing sentence also retells John 1:1-2 by describing "the Word who was with God in the beginning." The citation does not cover everything the card tells.

The comment that someone in the crowd has been reading their Scriptures uses the doubters' appeal to Scripture in verse 42, but the card cites only verse 41. The citation should extend through John 7:42.
The first sentence uses Jesus' statement in John 8:7, and the second tells what happens in John 8:8, but the card cites only John 8:8. Its citation should cover John 8:7-8.

The observation that the men from Cyprus and Cyrene are never named uses Acts 11:20, while the hand of the Lord being with them uses Acts 11:21. Citing only Acts 11:21 is too narrow; this story card's range should begin at verse 20.
The opening sentence, "So Paul's got a day job now," uses Paul's work from Acts 18:3, but the card cites only Acts 18:4.
The statement that Paul has been opposed and insulted in Corinth retells Acts 18:6, but the card cites only Acts 18:9.
The statement that Paul never got a word in uses Acts 18:14, and the statement about the case's outcome also draws on Acts 18:15. Citing only Acts 18:16 does not cover everything the card tells.
The card retells the water becoming shallower, which comes from Acts 27:28, but its citation starts at Acts 27:29. The story-card citation is narrower than the verses it uses.

The card calls "not even one" the second occurrence, which uses the first occurrence in Romans 3:10 as well as the material in Romans 3:11-12. Its citation should therefore begin at Romans 3:10 rather than Romans 3:11.
The card quotes "the least of the apostles" from verse 9 and "I am what I am" from verse 10, but its citation covers only verse 10. It should cite 1 Corinthians 15:9-10.
The card retells the open door for preaching from 2 Corinthians 2:12 as well as Paul's lack of peace from verse 13, but it cites only verse 13. Its citation should span 2 Corinthians 2:12-13.

The card recalls Paul leaving Troas with no peace from 2 Corinthians 2:13 before telling the thanksgiving and triumph of verse 14. Citing only verse 14 is too narrow; the card uses 2 Corinthians 2:13-14.
The card cites only 2 Corinthians 4:17, but its statement that Paul was "STRUCK DOWN" also uses 2 Corinthians 4:9. Its citation therefore does not cover every passage fact it uses.

The card retells that the mystery stayed hidden through earlier generations, which comes from Ephesians 3:5, but its citation covers only Ephesians 3:6. The citation should include every verse the card uses.
This card retells both verse 4's praying with joy and verse 5's reason for that joy, but it cites only verse 5. Its citation should begin with the first verse it uses.
The card retells standing firm from verse 27 and not being frightened by opponents from verse 28, but it cites only Philippians 1:28. Its citation should cover Philippians 1:27-28.

The card explicitly retells Colossians 1:6 when it says the gospel was bearing fruit and growing, as well as telling Colossians 1:10. Its citation of only Colossians 1:10 does not cover everything the card tells.
The résumé line repeats 'Firstborn over creation' from Colossians 1:15, but the card cites only Colossians 1:18. Its citation does not cover every verse the card uses.
The reminder that the Son is the image of the invisible God uses Colossians 1:15, but the card cites only Colossians 1:19. Its citation does not begin with the first verse it uses.
The first sentence retells Colossians 2:1 when it says Paul is struggling for people he has never met face to face, but the card cites only Colossians 2:2. Its citation should cover Colossians 2:1-2.

The second sentence says that Paul likewise does not give deacons the job until they have proven themselves. That already retells the testing-before-service movement of verse 10, so citing only verse 9 is narrower than what the card uses.

The card tells 1 Timothy 6:19 but also explicitly recalls 1 Timothy 6:12, where Paul told Timothy to take hold of eternal life. Its citation covers only 6:19, leaving out the earlier verse used in the comparison.
The opening clause "If God grants that" uses the condition from verse 25, while coming to their senses is from verse 26. Citing only verse 26 is narrower than the verses the card uses.

The transition explicitly uses the rulers from verse 1 as well as the move to how believers speak in verse 2, but the card cites only Titus 3:2. Its citation is too narrow and should begin at Titus 3:1.
The card says the writer quotes Jesus three times, but that count uses the two quotes in verse 13 as well as the quote in verse 12. The citation therefore ends one verse too early.
The card tells both that God rested at creation (Hebrews 4:4) and that the oath is repeated (Hebrews 4:5), but it cites only verse 5. Its citation should be Hebrews 4:4-5.

The description of Jesus as a high priest who knows what life down here is like retells Hebrews 4:15, while approaching the throne of grace tells Hebrews 4:16. The citation covers only Hebrews 4:16 instead of Hebrews 4:15-16.

The high priest being picked from regular people retells Hebrews 5:1, and his dealing gently with the ignorant and misguided tells Hebrews 5:2. The citation should therefore span Hebrews 5:1-2, not only Hebrews 5:2.
Saying that Christ was called just like Aaron uses the comparison with Aaron in Hebrews 5:4 as well as Christ's calling in Hebrews 5:5. The citation covers only Hebrews 5:5 instead of Hebrews 5:4-5.
The observation that "lose heart" appears again uses Hebrews 12:3 as well as Hebrews 12:5, but the card cites only Hebrews 12:5.
Saying that the writer gives "one more Therefore" uses the earlier Therefore in Hebrews 12:1 as well as the one in Hebrews 12:12, but the card cites only Hebrews 12:12.
The card retells the farmer waiting for rain from James 5:7, but its citation is only James 5:17. The citation does not cover all the passage material the card uses.
The opening clause retells verse 22 when it says John just mentioned keeping God's commandments, but the card cites only verse 23. Since the card uses both verses, its citation is too narrow.
The card uses "Forever and ever" from Revelation 11:15 before telling about the twenty-four elders in Revelation 11:16, but it cites only verse 16. Its range should begin at verse 15.
The card retells the dragon standing there and waiting from Revelation 12:4 as well as the birth and ruling statement from 12:5, but it cites only 12:5.
The opening clause retells the dragon being thrown down from Revelation 12:9 before telling 12:10, but the card cites only 12:10.

rule.text: A few discovery questions are fine. Some moments can't be reasoned out, like where Jonah's ship is headed. A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

examples: Five of the nine choice cards (3, 5, 8, 10 and 17) require unseen details that cannot be reasoned from the earlier cards: whether the word continues after Josiah, the exile, the nations, Jeremiah's objection and the rest of the job list. That leaves only four informed guesses, so most of this stop's choices are discoveries rather than informed guesses.

Discovery guesses dominate this stop. Card 2 asks for wine with no clue, card 6 asks whether the Rechabites drink before their command is known, card 7 introduces Jonadab only in the answers, and card 10 asks for Jonadab's reason without context. That is four of the stop's seven choice cards, so most are not informed guesses a baker can reason out from the earlier cards.

Six of the eight choice cards—2, 4, 5, 7, 9 and 12—ask for details that earlier cards neither supply nor make inferable: the writing material, Baruch's condition, the sorrow added to his pain, whose work is demolished, what Baruch is seeking and what the disaster strikes. Discovery questions consequently dominate the stop instead of remaining a few exceptions among mostly informed guesses.

Cards 3, 7, 9, 13 and 15 ask for direct revelation, a human form, human hands, the three animal faces or the spirit's leading before the earlier cards provide a sufficient basis for choosing. Five of the nine choices depend on discovery rather than reasoning, so informed guesses are not the dominant pattern.

Discovery questions recur beyond a small exception. For example, the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out a year in stop 1 card 8, Judah in stop 1 card 10, prophesying in stop 1 card 14, eating at set times in stop 2 card 4, or God's concession in stop 2 card 11. The location in stop 2 card 7 is likewise unrevealed. This recurring pattern makes too much of Prep depend on luck or prior knowledge rather than reasoned picks from the setups.

Cards 2, 4, 8, 10 and 16 require facts that the earlier cards do not help the baker infer: the lioness, the cub's violence, Egypt, the choice of another cub and Babylon. Five of the stop's nine choices are therefore discovery guesses, leaving only four informed guesses, so the permitted exceptions have become the majority.

Cards 2, 4 and 6 are all discovery questions: the earlier cards give no basis for choosing Rabbah, seeking an omen, or Jerusalem rather than Rabbah. Three of the stop's five choices therefore come down to luck, so most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses and the discovery questions go beyond the allowed few.

Most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses. Cards 2, 3, 9, 10, 16 and 17 ask for the idols, the absence of a prince, the broken body part, the lack of treatment, the sword's owner and the mortally wounded simile before the earlier cards give any basis for reasoning to those details. Six discovery guesses out of ten leaves only four informed choices.

Three of the stop's five choices depend on luck rather than an informed guess. Card 2 gives no basis for choosing what the people say, card 4 gives no basis for knowing whether they practice Ezekiel's words, and card 6 asks what their hearts pursue after the setup merely says they are chasing "something else." That makes most of this stop a guessing game rather than allowing only a few discovery questions.

Discovery questions dominate this stop. Cards 2, 4, 5, 9, 12 and 13 ask for unrevealed details that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards: Gabriel's name, what he gives Daniel, when the answer went out, the endpoint of the timeline, what happens to the Messiah, and whether the coming prince's people destroy the city and sanctuary. That is six of the stop's nine choice cards, leaving most picks dependent on luck or prior knowledge rather than reasoning from the walkthrough.

Five of the nine choice cards (4, 6, 10, 12 and 13) require outside knowledge or luck: the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out Judah's response, Ephraim's action with Assyria and Egypt, what Jacob grabs, what Jacob does after prevailing, or the location Bethel. This concentration makes most of the stop's choices discovery questions rather than informed guesses.

Too many choices require guessing details that the earlier cards have not supplied or made inferable. Cards 4-5 ask for two unrevealed parts of Amaziah's report, cards 11-12 ask about Amos's background and then his occupation without a useful clue, and cards 7 and 19 add further blind detail guesses. Discovery questions make up about half of the stop, including two consecutive pairs, rather than remaining a few exceptions among mostly informed guesses.

Too many choices are discoveries or coin flips for informed guesses to be the majority. Stop 1 card 5 asks about redemption in Babylon right after only the destination was established; stop 1 card 11 gives no basis for deciding who gets the wealth; stop 1 card 13 introduces the struck judge only in the question; and stop 2 card 3 introduces the ruler's eternal origins only in the question. Added to the picture, destination and town discovery questions, a baker using only the earlier cards must guess on about half of the choices.

Most choices are discoveries rather than informed guesses. Cards 4, 6, 10, 15 and 17 offer little or no basis in the earlier cards for reasoning out the answer; together with the unrevealed-detail blanks in cards 2 and 9, that makes seven of the ten choices dependent on prior knowledge or luck. Discovery questions therefore dominate the stop instead of being the few exceptions.

Discovery questions dominate the stop. Cards 2, 3, 6, 11, 13, 14, 16, 18 and 19 provide no earlier-card basis for reasoning out the answer, leaving only cards 7, 8 and 9 clearly grounded in what the baker has already learned.

Discovery questions are too frequent to remain the allowed exception. Stop 1 cards 2, 5, 8 and 9 ask for details that cannot be inferred from the earlier cards, and stop 2 cards 2, 6 and 11 likewise ask for unrevealed facts without an inferential setup. Consequently, too much of the walkthrough depends on prior knowledge or luck rather than informed reasoning.

Discovery questions make up at least half of the walkthrough rather than a few exceptions. Stop 1 cards 4, 8, 12, 16 and 17, and stop 2 cards 4, 6, 8, 11, 13 and 20, provide no earlier-card basis for reasoning out the answer. For example, the baker has no contextual way to determine who accompanies the LORD, whether the water flows year-round, which feast the survivors celebrate, or whether rain rather than manna or dew will be withheld.

Cards 2, 5, 6 and 7 give no earlier-card basis for choosing their answers: the extent of the healing, what God puts on the Servant, what He proclaims, and whether He quarrels and cries out are all unrevealed details. Four of the stop's seven choice cards are luck-based, including three consecutive guesses at Isaiah's wording, so this stop becomes a guessing game rather than relying mostly on informed guesses.

Most of the stop's choices are discovery questions rather than informed guesses. Before cards 2, 3, 6, 7 and 9, the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out the synagogue, the crowd's astonishment, the carpenter's-son question, Mary's name or whether Jesus's sisters are present. Five of nine choice cards therefore require prior knowledge or luck, which is more than the allowed few discovery questions.

Too many choices depend on luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 2, 4, 7, 14 and 16 provide no contextual basis for reasoning out the size of the gathering, the crown's material, the spitting, Golgotha's meaning or whether Jesus drinks after tasting. These five discovery questions outnumber the stop's informed guesses.

The same guessing pattern continues in cards 2, 3, 7, 13 and 14. The earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out casting lots, staying to keep watch, the robbers' identity, the leaders' trust-in-God taunt or whether the robbers join the mockery. Five of the stop's eight choices are therefore discoveries rather than informed guesses.

Discovery or coin-flip picks are too prevalent. Stop 1 cards 2, 4, 8 and 10, and stop 2 cards 2, 3, 7 and 13 withhold the crucial fact without giving earlier-card context from which to reason. These eight of the fourteen choice cards include guesses at the untranslated cry, the sponge's contents, the bystanders' response, the veil's fate and tearing direction, the saints' timing, and Mary Magdalene's presence. Informed guesses therefore do not clearly dominate the walkthrough.

Most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses. Cards 4, 7, 12, 13 and 14 ask for details that earlier cards neither supply nor make inferable: the kingdom being near, each pair of brothers' work, the timing of Jesus' call, and whether Zebedee is left alone. Card 2 is also a discovery question, while only cards 9 and 10 clearly provide enough setup for a reasoned pick.

Too many choices depend on luck rather than the earlier cards: how Jesus heals (6), the immediate timing (8), the warning's content (10), the priest and Moses details (11), the offering's purpose (12), and whether the man obeys (14) are not inferable from their setups. Six of the ten choice cards are discovery questions, so most choices are not informed guesses.

Too much of this stop relies on discovery rather than informed choices. Cards 2, 4, 5, 13, 14 and 18 require details that the earlier cards do not supply or imply: six of the stop's eleven choice cards, leaving most of its choices something other than informed guesses.

Too many choices depend on guessing unrevealed details. Cards 5, 7 and 9 provide no basis for reasoning out spit, incomplete sight or trees. Card 4 is also a guess because card 3 never says that Jesus led the man out of the village before asking whether He healed him in the village. That leaves only half of the stop's eight choice cards as informed guesses, rather than most of them.

Discovery questions dominate the walkthrough rather than remaining a few exceptions. For example, the name's origin (stop 1 card 2), the sacrifice (stop 1 card 7), Simeon's revelation (stop 1 card 9), what the Child is appointed to cause (stop 2 card 3), Anna's whereabouts (stop 2 card 10), the family's destination (stop 2 card 16), and Jesus' wisdom and grace (stop 2 card 18) all require new information that cannot be worked out from the earlier cards. Together with the other unsupported choices, this leaves most choices dependent on discovery or luck rather than reasoning.

Too many choices ask for the next unseen detail rather than an informed inference. The setups do not let the baker reason out the marketplace picture in card 2, the children's exact response in card 4, or the demon accusation in card 6, and card 10 is another unseen-word guess. Most of the stop therefore becomes a guessing game.

Too many of this stop's choices depend on luck rather than reasoning from the setup. Card 4 gives no basis for choosing the Gentiles, card 7 gives no basis for knowing what happens on the third day, and card 8 gives no indication that the disciples fail to understand. Thus at least three of the stop's five choices are discovery questions, so they dominate the stop instead of remaining occasional exceptions.

Discovery questions dominate this stop. Cards 2, 3, 5, 9 and 12 ask for a title, claim, reason, image or result that the earlier cards give the baker no basis for inferring. Five of the seven choice cards therefore depend on luck or prior knowledge rather than informed guesses.

Discovery or chance dominates this stop's choices. Card 5 gives no basis for inferring glorification, cards 7 and 9 ask for identifications without clues, card 10 requires recall of David and Bethlehem, and card 12 asks for an outcome that has not been set up. A few such discovery questions are allowed, but here most of the eight choices are not informed guesses.

Most of this stop's choices are discoveries or guesses rather than reasoned picks. Cards 2, 4 and 6 ask for Jesus' reason, gift and definition without setup from which the baker could infer them, and cards 8 and 10 are unsupported true-or-false guesses. Discovery questions dominate the stop instead of being the exception.

Six of the twelve choice cards in this stop (cards 2, 7, 10, 13, 16 and 19) require recall or luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards: there is no usable clue for Abraham's identity, the brothers' motive, the new king's behavior, Midian, the prophet being like Moses, or Babylon. That is more than a few discovery questions in one stop and leaves no more than half of its choices as informed guesses.

Five of the nine choice cards require information that earlier cards give no way to reason out: Stephen's vision in card 2, Saul's name in card 6, whether Stephen seeks judgment in card 10, the group that does not scatter in card 14, and the scattering locations in card 15. Discovery questions therefore make up most of this stop's choices instead of remaining a few exceptions.

Six of the nine choice cards (2, 4, 5, 7, 11 and 12) ask for an unrevealed destination, reason, outcome or biographical detail without earlier cards giving a basis to prefer the correct answer. Discovery questions therefore make up most of this stop's choices, rather than a few exceptions.

Too many choices depend on luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Card 2 gives no basis for knowing the unseen statement about Philip's daughters, card 5 gives no basis for identifying the belt's owner, card 6 asks for an unseen word in Agabus's prophecy with no basis for choosing among the three peoples, and card 10 offers three plausible responses without establishing what the friends conclude. These make four of the stop's seven choice cards discovery guesses, so most of its choices are not informed guesses.

Six of the ten choice cards require unrevealed facts to be guessed: cards 2, 4, 5, 10, 15 and 18 ask who brings the case, why the leaders want Paul summoned, how Festus responds, whether the charges can be proved, what Festus knows and how Festus answers the appeal without enough earlier context to reason out the answers. Discovery questions therefore outnumber the informed guesses instead of being just a few.

Too many choices in this stop depend on luck or prior Bible knowledge rather than the earlier cards. Cards 2, 3, 5, 9, 11, 13 and 15 introduce their answers without enough setup: for example, nothing before card 9 distinguishes Isaac from Ishmael, nothing before card 11 identifies Isaac's mother, and card 14's statement that election is not by works gives no basis for choosing whether the older or younger would serve in card 15. Seven of the stop's ten choices are therefore discovery questions, so most of its choices are not informed guesses.

Cards 2, 5, 6, 8 and 10 require the baker to predict Paul's next label, reason, detail or instruction without enough earlier context to infer it. Five of the stop's six choices consequently depend on discovery or luck rather than informed reasoning.

Too many choices depend on luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 2, 6, 7, 10, 12 and 16 ask for the schedule, the gift's carriers, its destination, Macedonia, the length of Paul's stay and the opposition without providing a basis for inferring those answers. This goes beyond a few discovery questions in a ten-choice stop.

This stop also relies too heavily on unrevealed answers. Cards 4, 6, 8, 13, 16 and 18 ask about Timothy's return, Apollos's decision, the word "love," the reason for Paul's gladness, the holy kiss and the curse without enough earlier context to reason those answers out. Consequently, most of the stop's choices are not informed guesses.

Too many choices depend on recall or luck rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 9, 11, 15, 17 and 18 do not provide enough setup to establish their answers, while cards 2 and 5 are additional discovery questions. Discovery questions therefore make up too large a share of the stop for most choices to be informed guesses.

Four of the seven choice cards are discovery guesses without enough context to reason toward an answer: card 2 asks Abraham's identity, card 4 asks what Abraham did, card 8 asks whether he was called God's friend, and card 11 asks what Rahab did. Only cards 6, 9 and 13 offer an informed basis for a pick, so most of this stop's choices are not informed guesses.

The stop relies on discovery questions beyond the allowed few. From the earlier cards, the baker cannot reason out the lion in card 4, the command to resist rather than run in card 6, what is true of brothers worldwide in card 7, Mark's identity in card 13, or the kiss of love in card 14. These require guessing unseen details, leaving most of the stop's choices without enough context for an informed pick.

Four of the stop's five choice cards are unsupported discovery questions. Cards 2, 6, 8 and 9 give the baker no earlier-card basis for reasoning out whether the account is secondhand, why the writer proclaims it, who the fellowship is with, or which additional purpose he gives. Discovery questions therefore dominate this stop rather than remaining a few exceptions.

Too many of this stop's ten choices depend on luck or prior knowledge rather than reasoning from the earlier cards. Cards 2, 3, 5, 8, 11, 12 and 14 ask for the angel, the extent of John's testimony, the scope of the blessing, the number of churches, sins, a kingdom and priests, or how many people will see Him without providing a basis for inferring those answers. These are not merely a few discovery questions among mostly informed guesses.

Cards 2, 4, 9 and 10 provide no earlier-card basis for reasoning out their answers: the First and the Last does not point to one of the three experiences, poverty does not make rich a reasoned pick, the prison setup gives no purpose, and no clue supports any duration. Four of the stop's seven choices therefore depend on discovery or luck, so most of its choices are not informed guesses.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

examples: The opening clause, “Twice they say no,” retells the refusals in Jeremiah 6:16-17, but the card cites only Jeremiah 6:18-19. Its citation therefore does not cover every verse the card uses; the recap needs its verses included or removed.
The card uses Jeremiah 22:18 for "No mourning for Jehoiakim" and Jeremiah 22:19 for the donkey burial, but it cites only Jeremiah 22:19.
The opening sentence uses Jeremiah 22:25, including Coniah being handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, before telling Jeremiah 22:26. The citation therefore starts too late.

rule.text: For who, which thing and where questions, wrong answers are real details from somewhere in the Bible, like Joppa when the right answer is Tarshish.

examples: This is a who question, but the wrong answer about kings carrying Zion's sons is not a real Bible detail. It combines the nations carrying her children in Isaiah 49:22 with the kings in Isaiah 49:23, rather than using a real detail as the distractor.
This is a "which animal" question, but "A dove caught in a net" is not a real detail from somewhere in the Bible. The wrong answers to this kind of question must be real Bible details.

For this which-thing question, the distractor 'His vineyard in Bethlehem' is an invented property-and-location pairing rather than a real detail from somewhere in the Bible. Bethlehem appears in Scripture, but a vineyard in Bethlehem is not an identifiable biblical detail.

rule.text: A few of those are okay, as long as most choice cards are informed guesses.

A baker who does not already know the passage has to guess.

Discovery and luck-based questions occur too often across both stops, rather than remaining a few exceptions among mostly informed guesses. For example, the earlier cards give no basis for reasoning out the attackers' direction (stop 1, card 4), what the LORD says about Israel and Judah (stop 1, card 8), where to tell the news (stop 1, card 18), which kings are stirred up (stop 2, card 2), what the LORD swears by (stop 2, card 7), or the content of the locust oath (stop 2, card 8). The setups commonly withhold a fact and immediately ask for it.
